description: We're a motivated team from India excited to build something real with NASA data at Space Apps 2026. We love solving real world problems with data, maps and clean web apps, and we aim to ship a working demo, not just slides. Looking for: Python/data analysis (pandas, GIS), web dev (JS/React), and a designer who can make our pitch video shine. Curious, committed beginners are welcome too!
summary:
Hots45 is a web application that turns two incompatible NASA satellite fire records into one consistent burning activity calendar for Asia (2003–2026). VIIRS, operating since 2012, detects about 4.7 times more hotspots than MODIS, so combining them naively creates a false jump in fire activity. We processed over 46 million FIRMS hotspots, fitted MODIS-to-VIIRS conversion factors for every 10° region and calendar month using the 2012–2021 overlap (R² = 0.988), and converted earlier MODIS years to the VIIRS scale, so the sensor of origin no longer matters. We also found that the Aqua satellite's orbit drift after 2021 biases MODIS counts, and excluded those years from the fit.

Users search any country, state or district and explore fires on an interactive 3D globe, burning calendar and timeline, comparing any month with its historical median. Using MODIS land cover, the app shows what is burning: 96% of Punjab–Haryana fires are on cropland. It also shows fire intensity, a backtested seasonal outlook, early-warning alerts and CSV downloads.

Emergency managers need to know when fire seasons start, how this year compares with normal, and where to act. With MODIS ageing and Suomi NPP ending in November 2026, a trustworthy harmonized record is essential.
details:
What it does
Hots45 is a web application that gives emergency managers one consistent, 23-year record of fire activity across Asia (2003–2026), built from NASA FIRMS active fire hotspots. Users search any country, state or district, explore fires on an interactive 3D globe and tilted map, and see a burning activity calendar (months × years), a zoomable timeline, the typical fire season, and how any month compares with its historical median. Results can be downloaded as CSV and PNG.

The problem
MODIS has observed fires since 2000. VIIRS, since 2012, has finer resolution and detects about 4.7 times more hotspots. Combining the two records naively creates a false jump in fire activity in 2012, which makes it impossible to say whether this year is worse than usual or how fire regimes are changing. With MODIS ageing and Suomi NPP ending in November 2026, the long-term record is at risk.

How it works

  1. Data: NASA FIRMS archive and near-real-time hotspots (MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS S-NPP C2), filtered to Asia (60–150°E, 11°S–55°N): over 46 million hotspots after cleaning.
  2. Cleaning: only vegetation fires and nominal/high-confidence detections are kept. Duplicates are removed, including overlaps between archive and near-real-time files. The record starts in 2003, the first full year with both MODIS satellites.
  3. Harmonization: hotspots are counted per 10° region and month. Using the 2012–2021 period, when both sensors observed the same places, we fitted a conversion factor (VIIRS ≈ k × MODIS) for every region and calendar month, falling back to an Asia-wide factor where data is sparse. MODIS counts before February 2012 are converted to the VIIRS scale, and from February 2012 real VIIRS counts are used, so the sensor of origin no longer matters. Converted MODIS matches real VIIRS with R² = 0.988.
  4. Analysis: for any area and period we compute the historical median, % difference from normal, z-score anomalies, typical season start, peak and end, and record years.
  5. Web app: a FastAPI backend queries Parquet files with DuckDB, answering any area query in under half a second. The frontend renders the globe, 3D columns, heatmap and anomaly maps, and the interactive charts.
  6. What is burning: each hotspot is labelled with the land cover at its location from NASA's MODIS MCD12Q1 product (IGBP classes, 500 m, previous year's map), grouped into cropland, forest, shrubland/savanna, grassland, wetland and other. This shows responders whether an area's fires are mainly crop-residue burning or forest fires, which need different responses.
  7. Fire intensity: Fire Radiative Power (FRP) is summed per region and month and harmonized with the same per-region, per-month method as hotspot counts, showing how much fire energy was released, not just how many fires.
  8. Seasonal outlook: for the next 1–3 months, the app gives a most-likely value and an 80% range for any area, combining the historical baseline, a statistically tested long-term trend, and how the current season is running. It was backtested on every month from 2015 to 2025 using only earlier data; where it does not beat a simple historical baseline, the app shows the baseline instead and says so.

What makes it creative and scientifically careful

  • We found and corrected a hidden bias. While validating, we discovered that the Aqua satellite’s orbit drift after 2021 shifted its overpass later into the afternoon fire peak, making MODIS see relatively more fires. The ratio of VIIRS to Aqua detections over Punjab fell from about 5 to 2.2. We fitted our factors only on the stable 2012–2021 years.
  • Validated against real events and ground data. The record clearly shows the 2015 Indonesian peat fires, the 2003 Siberian fires and the November 2021 Punjab stubble-burning record. Its sharp drop in Punjab fires in October 2026 matches official Punjab Pollution Control Board reports.
  • Transparent by design. Data gaps, provisional near-real-time data, partial years and MODIS-estimated periods are all clearly marked, so users know how much to trust each number.
  • “Compared to normal” views. Users see not just where fires are, but where activity is unusual for that time of year, which is what matters for early warning.
  • Honest forecasting. outlooks are given as ranges, validated by backtesting, with each area's reliability score shown to users.

Benefits and intended impact
Emergency responders, firefighters, land managers and pollution control boards can see when fire season usually starts and peaks in their district, whether this year is above normal, and which areas need attention, so they can deploy teams and warn hospitals earlier. Researchers and policymakers get a trustworthy long-term record to evaluate trends and policies such as stubble-burning bans. The method also carries forward to future satellites, such as NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 after Suomi NPP.

Factors we considered
Sensor differences, regional and seasonal variation, satellite orbit drift, data gaps and provisional data, duplicate detections, partial months, accessibility (colour-blind-safe palettes, readable charts), map borders for India (using India’s official point of view), performance on large data, and that our outputs are statistics, not official warnings. MCD12Q1 has no separate peatland class; FRP is not comparable between sensors at pixel level, so only totals are harmonized; outlooks do not yet include weather forecasts and are not official forecasts.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: Python, TypeScript, SQL
  • Data processing: pandas, NumPy, DuckDB, Apache Parquet (pyarrow), Matplotlib
  • Backend: FastAPI, Uvicorn, Docker
  • Frontend: React, Vite, deck.gl (3D globe and map), MapLibre GL, Apache ECharts, Tailwind CSS
  • Data and imagery: NASA FIRMS (MCD14ML, VNP14IMGML, FIRMS API), NASA GIBS Blue Marble and Black Marble, open administrative boundaries
  • Development: Git and GitHub, Vercel, VS Code, AI coding assistant (Claude Code)
